question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Head in the clouds
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Being absent minded.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Head in the clouds" means to be absent-minded, impractical, or out of touch with reality; to be lost in one's own thoughts, fantasies or daydreams rather than paying attention to what is actually happening. (खयालों में खोए रहना / अव्यावहारिक होना)
◦ Example: Ever since he won the lottery, he has had his head in the clouds and can't focus on his job.

• The phrase draws on the image of someone whose head is literally up among the clouds — too high up and detached to notice or deal with things happening on the ground.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Being extremely tall is a literal, physical description and has nothing to do with the idiomatic sense of "head in the clouds."

• Option 3: Being extremely happy is closer to idioms like "on cloud nine" or "walking on air", not "head in the clouds."

• Option 4: Being extremely sad is closer to idioms like "down in the dumps" or "feeling blue", not "head in the clouds."

NOTE

• Do not confuse "head in the clouds" (impractical/daydreaming) with "on cloud nine" (extremely happy) — both use "cloud(s)" but mean very different things.

• Other commonly asked idioms of impracticality/distraction: "lost in thought", "in a world of one's own", and "to build castles in the air" (to have unrealistic plans/dreams).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank.
I ________ (itemise) the work that will have to be done.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. enumerate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "itemise" means to list things one by one, or to record item by item, and its closest synonym among the options is "enumerate," which means to mention or list a number of things one by one. (एक-एक करके गिनाना / सूचीबद्ध करना)
◦ Example: I enumerated the work that will have to be done before the deadline.

• Applying this to the sentence: "I enumerate (itemise) the work that will have to be done" makes complete sense — the speaker is listing out the tasks one by one.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Impart means to give or communicate (information, knowledge, or a quality) to someone, not to list things. (प्रदान करना)

• Option 3: Conceal means to hide or keep something secret, which is the opposite of listing things out openly. (छिपाना)

• Option 4: Assess means to evaluate or judge the nature, quality or amount of something, not simply to list it. (आकलन करना)

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "enumerate" useful for SSC: "catalogue," "tabulate," "specify" and "detail."

• Do not confuse "enumerate" (to list) with "numerate" (able to work confidently with numbers).

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A. have seen a major blow
B. the last two years
C. people and lower-income countries
D. to the world's economy and
E. were hit particularly hard
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. BADCE.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Arranging the parts as B-A-D-C-E gives a grammatically correct and meaningful sentence: "The last two years have seen a major blow to the world's economy and people and lower-income countries were hit particularly hard."

• Rule for sentence rearrangement: First identify the subject/starting point of the sentence (here, B: "the last two years", which naturally begins the sentence as the time-subject), then find the part that logically continues it as its verb phrase (A: "have seen a major blow"), followed by the object of that blow (D: "to the world's economy and"), and finally the two linked consequences (C: "people and lower-income countries" and E: "were hit particularly hard"), since C and E together form one clause (subject + verb) that must stay adjacent and in that order.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: BCADE is incorrect because it places C ("people and lower-income countries") directly after B, breaking the required subject-verb link between B and A, and produces a meaningless sequence.

• Option 2: EBCAD is incorrect because it starts with E ("were hit particularly hard"), a verb phrase with no subject before it, making the sentence ungrammatical from the start.

• Option 4: ADBEC is incorrect because it starts with A ("have seen a major blow") without a subject, and separates C and E, which must remain together as a single subject-verb unit.

NOTE

• In parts-rearrangement questions, always locate the independent clause's subject first, then its main verb, and keep any linked subject-verb pair (like C-E here) adjacent.

• Read the fully reconstructed sentence aloud mentally to confirm it makes complete logical and grammatical sense before finalising the order.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Extract
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Insert.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Extract" means to remove or take out (something), typically by effort or force. (निकालना)
◦ Example: The dentist had to extract the decayed tooth.

• Its most appropriate antonym among the given options is "Insert," which means to put or fit (something) into something else; to place in. (डालना / अंदर रखना)
◦ Example: Please insert the key into the lock before turning it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Fry means to cook something in hot oil or fat, which is unrelated to the idea of removing or inserting. (तलना)

• Option 3: Cut means to divide or open something with a sharp-edged tool; while it can loosely relate to "extract," it does not express the opposite meaning of "taking out." (काटना)

• Option 4: Pull means to exert force on something to move it towards oneself, which is close in action to "extract" itself, not its opposite. (खींचना)

NOTE

• Other common antonym pairs based on "extract" (उद्धरण/निकालना): extract ↔ insert, remove ↔ add, withdraw ↔ deposit.

• "Extract" also has a noun sense meaning a short passage taken from a book or piece of music; do not confuse this with the verb sense being tested here.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.
Although he was exhausted from working all day, John continues to study for his upcoming exam.
option_1: will continue to study for his upcoming exam
option_2: has been studying for his upcoming exam
option_3: continued to study for his upcoming exam
option_4: continues studying for his upcoming exam
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. continued to study for his upcoming exam.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence begins with "Although he was exhausted from working all day...", which is in the Simple Past Tense. For grammatical consistency, the verb in the main clause describing the same time frame must also be in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Tense Consistency in a Sentence: When one clause of a sentence is set in the past, the other clause(s) describing events in the same time frame must also use past forms, unless there is a clear reason (such as a universal truth or a clearly marked shift in time) to change tense.

• Applying the rule: "continues" (Simple Present) must be changed to "continued" (Simple Past) to match "was exhausted." The rest of the phrase, "to study for his upcoming exam," stays unchanged as it correctly follows the past-tense verb.
◦ Corrected: Although he was exhausted from working all day, John continued to study for his upcoming exam.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "will continue to study for his upcoming exam" wrongly shifts the sentence into the Future Tense, which does not agree with the past-tense clause "was exhausted."

• Option 2: "has been studying for his upcoming exam" uses the Present Perfect Continuous Tense, which again does not match the Simple Past Tense of the first clause.

• Option 4: "continues studying for his upcoming exam" keeps the verb in the Simple Present Tense, which still fails to agree with "was exhausted" (Simple Past).

NOTE

• Always check the tense of the reference clause in a sentence-improvement question and match the tense of the underlined part to it, unless the sentence gives explicit reason otherwise (such as "always," "every day," or a universal fact).

• "Continue" can be followed by either a to-infinitive ("continued to study") or a gerund ("continued studying") with no real difference in meaning — but the tense of "continue" itself must still agree with the rest of the sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Assuagement
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Mollification.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Assuagement" means the act of easing, soothing, calming or relieving (a pain, feeling, or desire). (शांत करना / राहत)
◦ Example: A short walk gave him some assuagement of his stress.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Mollification," which means the act of appeasing, calming down, or softening someone's anger or distress. (शांत करना / नरम करना)
◦ Example: His apology served as a mollification of her anger.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Consignment means a batch of goods sent or delivered to someone, an entirely unrelated commercial term. (माल की खेप)

• Option 2: Stratification means the arrangement or classification of something into layers or levels, unrelated to soothing or calming. (स्तरीकरण)

• Option 3: Ruthlessness means having or showing no pity or compassion for others, which is nearly opposite in feeling to "assuagement." (निर्दयता)

NOTE

• Word family: assuage (verb) → assuagement (noun); similarly, mollify (verb) → mollification (noun).

• Other synonyms of "assuage/mollify" useful for SSC: "alleviate," "placate," "pacify," "appease" and "soothe."

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
One needs to be free of prejudices while dealing with judicial cases.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Equalities.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Prejudices" means preconceived opinions or biases against a person or group, formed without adequate reason or knowledge, usually unfavourable. (पूर्वाग्रह)
◦ Example: A good judge must set aside all personal prejudices while deciding a case.

• Its most appropriate antonym among the options is "Equalities," which refers to the state of being equal, of treating everyone the same way without bias or favour, the opposite of holding a prejudiced/biased view. (समानता)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Favours refers to acts of kindness or partiality shown to someone, which is itself a form of bias rather than its opposite. (पक्षपात)

• Option 2: Discriminations means unjust or prejudicial treatment based on categories such as race, age, or sex, which is a near-synonym of "prejudices," not its antonym. (भेदभाव)

• Option 3: Bigotries means intolerant, obstinate devotion to one's own opinions and prejudices, again a synonym of "prejudices," not its opposite. (कट्टरता)

NOTE

• Related word family: prejudiced (adjective) ↔ impartial/unbiased/unprejudiced (antonyms).

• Other useful antonym pairs on this theme: bias ↔ fairness, bigotry ↔ tolerance, discrimination ↔ equality.

question:
Select the meaningful and correctly spelt word from the options to fill in the blank.
The song composed by the choir for the special programme was an _________ one.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. imitated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Imitated" — the past participle of "imitate," meaning copied or made to resemble something else; not original or genuine.
◦ Example: The song composed by the choir for the special programme was an imitated one, based on an old folk tune.

• Spelling key: I-M-I-T-A-T-E-D. Note there is a single "t" in "imi-" and the word ends in "-tated," derived from the Latin imitari, meaning "to copy."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "imiteitted" is not a valid English word at all — it garbles both the middle and ending of "imitated."

• Option 2: "emittated" is not a valid English word; it wrongly blends "emit" with an incorrect "-tated" ending, and does not fit the meaning of the sentence.

• Option 3: "eradicated" is a correctly spelled real word, meaning completely destroyed or got rid of, but it does not fit the meaning of the sentence — a song cannot logically be described as "an eradicated one."

NOTE

• Related words: imitate (verb), imitation (noun), imitative (adjective), imitator (a person who imitates).

• Always check both spelling accuracy and contextual meaning in fill-in-the-blank spelling questions — a correctly spelled word that does not fit the sentence is still the wrong answer.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Philolegy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling of the word is "Philology," meaning the study of the structure, historical development, and relationships of languages, not "Philolegy."

• Spelling key: the word is built from the Greek roots philo- (loving) + -logy (study of), so it must end in "-logy," not "-legy." The incorrect option wrongly swaps the "o" for an "e" in the suffix.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Philosophy" is correctly spelled, meaning the study of the fundamental nature of knowledge, reality and existence.

• Option 2: "Philanthropy" is correctly spelled, meaning the practice of helping others, especially through charitable donations.

• Option 4: "Philately" is correctly spelled, meaning the collection and study of postage stamps.

NOTE

• All four options share the Greek prefix "philo-" meaning "loving/fond of": philo-sophy (loving wisdom), philo-logy (loving language/learning), philanthropy (loving mankind), and philately (from Greek "philo-" + "ateleia," love of exemption from tax, referring to prepaid postage).

• Common "-logy" ending words to watch spelling on: biology, geology, zoology, psychology, technology.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
Access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene is a human right—fundamental to everyone's health, dignity and prosperity.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. grace.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "Dignity" means a state or quality of being worthy of honour or respect; a calm, serious and controlled manner or bearing. (गरिमा / प्रतिष्ठा)
◦ Example: The old man carried himself with great dignity despite his poverty.

• Its closest synonym among the given options is "Grace," which here means elegance, poise, and a sense of honour or refined bearing, closely aligned with the idea of dignity. (शालीनता / गरिमा)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Enthusiasm means intense and eager enjoyment, interest, or approval, unrelated to the idea of dignity or respect. (उत्साह)

• Option 2: Immorality means the state of not conforming to accepted standards of morality; wickedness, which is nearly opposite to the respectful sense of "dignity." (अनैतिकता)

• Option 4: Wealth means an abundance of valuable possessions or money, an entirely different concept from dignity. (धन-संपत्ति)

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "dignity" useful for SSC: "nobility," "honour," "self-respect," and "stateliness."

• Antonym of "dignity": "indignity" or "disgrace," meaning a loss of honour or self-respect.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Were this boy / washing his clothes / yesterday when the matron / came for a regular round?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Were this boy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "Were this boy" contains a subject-verb agreement error. The subject "this boy" is third person singular, so it must take the singular auxiliary verb "was," not the plural "were."

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement with "Be": A singular subject (he/she/it/this + singular noun) takes was/is; a plural subject (they/we/these + plural noun) takes were/are.
◦ Corrected: Was this boy washing his clothes yesterday when the matron came for a regular round?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "washing his clothes" is grammatically correct — it is the present participle correctly used with the Past Continuous Tense structure "was/were + V-ing."

• Option 2: "yesterday when the matron" is grammatically correct — "yesterday" appropriately signals the past time frame, and "when the matron" correctly introduces the subordinate clause.

• Option 4: "came for a regular round" is grammatically correct — "came" is the correct Simple Past Tense form of "come," matching the past time frame of the sentence.

NOTE

• Common SSC trap: interrogative sentences beginning with "Was/Were" must still follow standard subject-verb agreement rules just like statements — check the number (singular/plural) of the subject that follows.

• Other frequently tested singular subjects that take "was," not "were": each, either, neither, everyone, somebody, this/that + noun.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the following sentence.
My parents had not call me yesterday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. did not call.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "My parents had not call me yesterday" is grammatically incorrect. The time marker "yesterday" signals the Simple Past Tense, not the Past Perfect Tense, and the given verb form "had not call" is itself an incomplete/incorrect verb form.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense (Negative): Subject + did not + V1 (base form of the verb).
◦ Applying the rule: My parents did not call me yesterday.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "does not calling" is incorrect — it mixes the Simple Present auxiliary "does" with the incorrect "-ing" form, and does not agree with the past time marker "yesterday."

• Option 3: "do not call" is incorrect — "do not" is a Simple Present Tense negative form, which cannot be used with the past time marker "yesterday."

• Option 4: "have not call" is incorrect — "have not" requires a past participle (V3), i.e., "have not called," and even then, the Present Perfect Tense cannot be used with a definite past time marker like "yesterday."

NOTE

• A definite past time expression such as "yesterday," "last week," "in 2020" always requires the Simple Past Tense, and is never used with the Present Perfect or Past Perfect Tense.

• Simple Past negative structure: did not (didn't) + base form (V1), regardless of the subject's person or number.

question:
Select the grammatically correct version of the following sentence.
This phone is inferior of that one.
option_1: This phone is inferior than that one.
option_2: This phone is more inferior than that one.
option_3: This phone is more inferior of that one.
option_4: This phone is inferior to that one.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. This phone is inferior to that one.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Inferior" is a Latin comparative adjective (like superior, junior, senior, prior). Such adjectives already carry a comparative sense within them and are never used with "more" or "than." Instead, they are followed by the preposition "to."

• Rule — Latin Comparatives: Superior, inferior, junior, senior, prior, posterior, exterior, interior + "to" (never "than" or "of").
◦ Correct: This phone is inferior to that one.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "This phone is inferior than that one." is incorrect because "inferior," being a Latin comparative, must be followed by "to," never "than."

• Option 2: "This phone is more inferior than that one." is incorrect for two reasons: it wrongly adds "more" before "inferior" (a double comparative), and it wrongly uses "than" instead of "to."

• Option 3: "This phone is more inferior of that one." is incorrect because it wrongly adds "more" before "inferior," and additionally uses the wrong preposition "of" instead of "to."

NOTE

• Other Latin comparatives that take "to": superior to, senior to, junior to, prior to, preferable to.

• Never use "more" before a Latin comparative adjective — "more superior," "more inferior," and "more senior" are all incorrect.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
One cannot exactly predict the way she behaves in public gatherings.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. prefigure.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "Predict" means to say or estimate that a specified thing will happen in the future. (भविष्यवाणी करना)
◦ Example: One cannot exactly prefigure the way she behaves in public gatherings.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Prefigure," which means to foreshadow or indicate something in advance; to represent or suggest beforehand, essentially to predict or foretell. (पूर्वाभास कराना / पहले से संकेत देना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Deliberate means to think about or discuss something carefully, or done consciously and intentionally, unrelated to foretelling the future. (सोच-समझकर करना)

• Option 2: Precipitate means to cause (an event or situation) to happen suddenly or sooner than expected, which refers to causing an event, not predicting it. (जल्दबाज़ी में होना)

• Option 4: Proliferate means to increase rapidly in number; to multiply, unrelated to the idea of prediction. (तेज़ी से बढ़ना)

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "predict" useful for SSC: "foretell," "forecast," "prophesy," and "anticipate."

• Do not confuse "prefigure" (to foreshadow) with "configure" (to arrange the parts of something) or "figure" (to calculate/appear).

question:
Select the word which means the same as the group of words underlined in the given sentence.
Vatsal is a lover and collector of books.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. bibliophile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase "lover and collector of books" is expressed in a single word as "bibliophile" — a person who loves and collects books. (पुस्तक-प्रेमी)
◦ Example: Vatsal is a bibliophile.

• Word formation: biblio- (Greek for "book") + -phile (Greek for "lover/one who is fond of") = a lover of books.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Anglophile means a person who greatly admires England and English customs, unrelated to books. (अंग्रेज़ी सभ्यता प्रेमी)

• Option 2: Recluse means a person who lives alone and avoids other people, unrelated to loving books. (एकांतवासी)

• Option 4: Polyglot means a person who knows and can use several languages, which is different from someone who loves/collects books. (बहुभाषाविद)

NOTE

• Other common "-phile" one-word substitutions for SSC: cynophile (lover of dogs), audiophile (lover of high-quality sound), francophile (admirer of France/French culture), technophile (lover of technology).

• Do not confuse "bibliophile" (lover of books) with "bibliographer" (a person who compiles bibliographies/lists of books).

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom for the underlined segment in the following sentence.
We should protect ourselves from jealous people.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Green-eyed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Green-eyed" means jealous or envious, often used in the fuller expression "the green-eyed monster," a phrase for jealousy popularised by Shakespeare. (ईर्ष्यालु)
◦ Example: We should protect ourselves from green-eyed people.

• The colour green has long been associated with envy/jealousy in English idiom, likely from the pallor or sickly look once believed to accompany strong jealousy.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: High-spirited means lively, energetic and cheerful, unrelated to jealousy.

• Option 2: Any Tom, Dick or Harry means any ordinary person chosen at random, unrelated to jealousy.

• Option 3: One trick pony means a person or thing with only one special feature, skill, or talent, unrelated to jealousy.

NOTE

• The phrase "the green-eyed monster" comes from Shakespeare's play Othello, where jealousy is described this way.

• Other idioms/phrases meaning jealous or envious: "eaten up with envy," and "sour grapes" (pretending not to want something you cannot have, related to envy).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The most important fruit in Kinnaur is apricot. It is possible to get it at everyplace in huge amount.
option_1: found for a huge amount everywhere
option_2: found everywhere in a huge amount
option_3: found everywhere with a huge amount
option_4: find everywhere in a huge amount
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. found everywhere in a huge amount.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "possible to get it at everyplace in huge amount" is awkward and grammatically flawed — "everyplace" is not standard English (it should be "everywhere"), and "in huge amount" needs the article "a" before "huge amount."

• Rule — Idiomatic and Grammatical Correctness: A sentence-improvement answer must (i) use standard, idiomatic word forms ("everywhere," not "everyplace"), and (ii) use correct article/preposition usage ("in a huge amount," not "in huge amount").
◦ Corrected: The most important fruit in Kinnaur is apricot. It is found everywhere in a huge amount.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "found for a huge amount everywhere" is incorrect because "found for a huge amount" wrongly suggests the fruit is sold "for" a large sum of money, distorting the intended meaning (that it is abundantly available).

• Option 3: "found everywhere with a huge amount" is incorrect because the preposition "with" does not fit; it should be "in" a huge amount.

• Option 4: "find everywhere in a huge amount" is incorrect because it uses the base form "find" instead of the passive form "found," which does not agree with the subject "It" in the passive construction "It is found..."

NOTE

• "Everywhere" is the standard adverb of place; "everyplace" is considered informal/non-standard and should be avoided in formal SSC English.

• Watch article usage with quantity expressions: "in a huge amount," "in a large quantity," "in great numbers" all require the article "a"/"an" before the noun phrase.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A) fourth floor of
B) nasty man named Mr. Douglas
C) an apartment building
D) there is a very mean,
E) who lives on the
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. D, B, E, A, C.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Arranging the parts as D-B-E-A-C produces the grammatically correct and meaningful sentence: "There is a very mean, nasty man named Mr. Douglas who lives on the fourth floor of an apartment building."

• Rule for sentence rearrangement: Begin with the part that introduces the subject of the sentence (D: "there is a very mean,", an existential "there is" construction), followed immediately by the noun phrase it introduces (B: "nasty man named Mr. Douglas"), then the relative clause describing him (E: "who lives on the"), followed by the specific location (A: "fourth floor of") and finally the building being referred to (C: "an apartment building").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: B, C, A, D, E is incorrect because it begins directly with B ("nasty man named Mr. Douglas") without the introductory "there is a very mean," making the sentence start abruptly and ungrammatically.

• Option 3: E, A, D, B, C is incorrect because it starts with E ("who lives on the"), a relative pronoun clause with no antecedent noun before it, which is ungrammatical as an opening.

• Option 4: C, B, A, E, D is incorrect because it starts with C ("an apartment building") with no verb or subject structure preceding it, and disconnects the "there is" construction from its noun phrase.

NOTE

• In "there is/there are" sentence-rearrangement questions, the part containing "there is/are" almost always comes first, immediately followed by the noun phrase it introduces.

• Keep descriptive/relative clauses (introduced by "who," "which," "that") directly after the noun they describe.

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in passive voice.
Does she still love you?
option_1: Are you still loved by her?
option_3: Is she still loved by you?
option_4: Are you still loving by her?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Are you still loved by her?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Does she still love you?" is an interrogative sentence in the Simple Present Tense, with subject "she" and object "you."

• Rule — Passive Voice of a Simple Present Interrogative (Yes/No question):
◦ Active: Does + Subject + V1 + Object?
◦ Passive: Is/Am/Are + Object + V3 + by + Subject?

• Applying the rule: the object "you" becomes the subject of the passive sentence and takes the auxiliary "are"; the verb "love" becomes the past participle "loved"; and the subject "she" becomes the agent "by her." The adverb "still" keeps its position before the past participle.
◦ Passive: Are you still loved by her?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Do you still love her?" is incorrect — it is simply a rewritten active-voice question with subject and object swapped, not a genuine passive-voice sentence.

• Option 3: "Is she still loved by you?" is incorrect — it wrongly keeps "she" as the one being loved and "you" as the agent, reversing the original meaning of the sentence.

• Option 4: "Are you still loving by her?" is incorrect — it wrongly uses the present participle "loving" instead of the past participle "loved," which is ungrammatical in passive voice.

NOTE

• For Yes/No questions, the auxiliary verb (is/am/are/does/do) always comes first, both in active and passive voice.

• Common error to avoid: using the "-ing" form instead of the past participle (V3) when forming the passive — only V3 is used after is/am/are/was/were/been.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
It is time to take tea.
option_1: It is time for the tea to be taken.
option_2: It is time tea must have been taken.
option_3: It is time we should take the tea.
option_4: It is time the tea has to be taken by us.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. It is time for the tea to be taken.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "It is time to take tea" uses the structure "It is time + to-infinitive," a common way of saying that the moment has come for an action to be performed.

• Rule — Passive Voice with "It is time + to-infinitive":
◦ Active: It is time + to + V1 + Object.
◦ Passive: It is time + for + Object + to be + V3.

• Applying the rule: the object "tea" is placed after "for," and the active verb "take" becomes the passive infinitive "to be taken."
◦ Passive: It is time for the tea to be taken.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "It is time tea must have been taken." is incorrect because it wrongly introduces the modal perfect "must have been taken," which changes both the meaning and the tense structure of the original sentence.

• Option 3: "It is time we should take the tea." is incorrect because it remains in the active voice (with subject "we" performing the action), not the passive voice required by the question.

• Option 4: "It is time the tea has to be taken by us." is incorrect because it unnecessarily introduces the agent "by us" (not present or implied in the original) and changes the structure to "has to be taken" instead of the correct infinitive passive "to be taken."

NOTE

• The construction "It is time + for + Object + to be + V3" is a fixed pattern frequently tested by SSC for converting "It is time to + V1 + Object" sentences into the passive voice.

• Similar fixed patterns: "It is time for someone to do something" (active with a different subject) versus "It is time for something to be done" (passive).

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I know these authors to _____1_____ outstanding individuals and remarkable teachers and consultants and have even_____2_____ them work their magic in training seminars, but I didn't know if they _____3_____ take this complex topic and fit into a book. They did. I _____4_____ you to really dig into this material, to pause and think deeply about each part and how the parts are _____5_____.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. be.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank fits into the structure **"I know these authors to _____ outstanding individuals...", which follows the pattern "know + object + to be + complement,"** used to state a fact or opinion about someone/something.

• Rule — Verb + Object + to be + Complement: Verbs like know, consider, believe, think, find are often followed by an object and the infinitive "to be" plus a noun/adjective complement, e.g., "I know him to be honest."
◦ Applying the rule: "I know these authors to be outstanding individuals and remarkable teachers..."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "been" is the past participle form of "be" and cannot follow "to" directly in this infinitive construction — "to been" is not grammatically valid.

• Option 3: "had" does not fit the required infinitive structure "to + base verb" after "know...authors," and produces an ungrammatical sentence.

• Option 4: "is" is a finite verb form and cannot follow the infinitive marker "to," which always requires the base form of the verb.

NOTE

• The infinitive marker "to" is always followed by the base form (V1) of the verb, never a finite form like "is/was" or a past participle like "been."

• Similar constructions frequently tested by SSC: "believe/consider/think + object + to be + complement."

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I know these authors to _____1_____ outstanding individuals and remarkable teachers and consultants and have even_____2_____ them work their magic in training seminars, but I didn't know if they _____3_____ take this complex topic and fit into a book. They did. I _____4_____ you to really dig into this material, to pause and think deeply about each part and how the parts are _____5_____.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. seen.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank follows the auxiliary **"have even_____", requiring the past participle (V3) form of the verb to complete the Present Perfect Tense**.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense: Subject + have/has + V3 (past participle) + Object.
◦ Applying the rule: "...and have even seen them work their magic in training seminars..." — here "seen" is the past participle of "see," correctly used after "have."

• The structure "seen them work" (bare infinitive after the object, following a verb of perception like "see") is also a correctly formed pattern in English: see/watch/hear + object + base verb.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "seeing" is the present participle (V-ing) form; it cannot directly follow "have" to form the Present Perfect Tense, which requires "have/has + V3."

• Option 3: "see" is the base form (V1); using "have even see" is grammatically incorrect, as "have" must be followed by a past participle, not a base form.

• Option 4: "saw" is the Simple Past Tense form (V2); it cannot follow "have," which strictly requires the past participle (V3) form.

NOTE

• Verbs of perception (see, watch, hear, notice, feel) are followed by an object and either the base form (for a complete action) or the "-ing" form (for an ongoing action): "seen them work" (complete) vs. "seen them working" (in progress) — both are valid, but only the base form matches the intended meaning here.

• Common irregular verb forms to remember: see – saw – seen; do not confuse the Simple Past (saw) with the Past Participle (seen).

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I know these authors to _____1_____ outstanding individuals and remarkable teachers and consultants and have even_____2_____ them work their magic in training seminars, but I didn't know if they _____3_____ take this complex topic and fit into a book. They did. I _____4_____ you to really dig into this material, to pause and think deeply about each part and how the parts are _____5_____.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. could.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The main clause "I didn't know" is in the Simple Past Tense. According to the Sequence of Tenses, the subordinate clause that follows must also be in a past form.

• Rule — Sequence of Tenses: When the main/principal clause of a sentence is in the past tense, the subordinate clause must also generally be in one of the past tenses; the modal "can" must change to "could" in a dependent clause governed by a past-tense main verb.
◦ Applying the rule: "...but I didn't know if they could take this complex topic and fit into a book."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "had" does not fit the required structure "if they _____ take," since "had take" is not a grammatically valid modal-verb combination (it would need "had taken," which changes the intended meaning to Past Perfect).

• Option 2: "are" does not fit — "are take" is ungrammatical, as "are" cannot be directly followed by the base form "take."

• Option 3: "have" does not fit the past-tense requirement of the sentence, and "have take" is not a valid verb combination (it would need "have taken").

Only the modal "could" correctly fits both the grammar and the past sequence of tenses.

NOTE

• Common modal shifts under the Sequence of Tenses when the reporting/main verb is in the past: can → could, will → would, may → might, shall → should.

• The Sequence of Tenses rule is a frequently tested SSC grammar topic, especially in cloze passages and direct-indirect speech conversions.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I know these authors to _____1_____ outstanding individuals and remarkable teachers and consultants and have even_____2_____ them work their magic in training seminars, but I didn't know if they _____3_____ take this complex topic and fit into a book. They did. I _____4_____ you to really dig into this material, to pause and think deeply about each part and how the parts are _____5_____.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. encourage.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb that logically fits **"I _____ you to really dig into this material, to pause and think deeply..." — the author is urging/motivating the reader to engage deeply with the book, which matches the meaning of "encourage."**

• Word meaning: "Encourage" means to give support, confidence, or hope to someone; to urge or persuade someone to do something.
◦ Example: I encourage you to really dig into this material.

• Grammar pattern: encourage + object + to + V1 is a standard verb pattern, correctly matching the sentence structure "I encourage you to really dig into this material."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "contradict" means to deny or oppose (a statement) as being false; to be in conflict with, which does not logically fit a context of urging someone to engage with a book.

• Option 2: "deny" means to state that something is not true; to refuse to give someone something, which contradicts the positive, encouraging tone of the passage.

• Option 4: "think" does not fit grammatically or logically in this slot — "I think you to really dig into" is not an idiomatic or standard English construction ("think" does not take this object + to-infinitive pattern in this sense).

NOTE

• The verb pattern "encourage/urge/persuade/advise + object + to + V1" is commonly tested in SSC cloze and error-spotting questions.

• Do not confuse "encourage" (to support/motivate) with "discourage" (to dishearten or deter someone from doing something) — the two are direct antonyms.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I know these authors to _____1_____ outstanding individuals and remarkable teachers and consultants and have even_____2_____ them work their magic in training seminars, but I didn't know if they _____3_____ take this complex topic and fit into a book. They did. I _____4_____ you to really dig into this material, to pause and think deeply about each part and how the parts are _____5_____.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. sequenced.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the sentence **"...to pause and think deeply about each part and how the parts are _____." — the passage is about a book made up of parts/topics arranged in a particular order, so the most logical word is "sequenced," meaning arranged in a particular order.**

• Word meaning: "Sequenced" means arranged or ordered in a particular series or succession.
◦ Example: The reader is encouraged to think about how the parts of the book are sequenced.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "recalled" means brought back into one's mind; remembered, which does not fit the context of describing how the parts of the book relate to one another in order.

• Option 3: "jumbled" means mixed up in a confused or disordered way, which contradicts the passage's positive tone about a carefully structured book.

• Option 4: "tinkered" means attempted to repair or improve something in a casual or desultory way, which does not logically describe how the "parts" of a well-structured book are arranged.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always check the overall tone and logical flow of the paragraph (here, praise for a well-organised book) before selecting a word — an option that is grammatically valid but tonally or logically inconsistent is still incorrect.

• Related words: sequence (noun/verb), sequential (adjective), consecutive, ordered, arranged — all convey the idea of a logical order or series.
